To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cigarette smoke causes a reduction in CFTR activity and expression at the plasma membrane of airway cells through a Ca2+ dependent process involving dynamin and calcineurine.
cigarette smoke exposure to airway cells causes a reduction in CFTR activity and cell surface expression which is linked to an increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+.
cigarette smoke causes an increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+ that induces dynamin- and Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase-dependent internalisation of the apical epithelial chloride channel, CFTR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of CFTR in epithelial cell membranes and the effects of this upon the airway surface.
the regulation of CFTR by cytosolic Ca(2+) and the mechanisms involved.
how the airway epithelial cell responds to the presence of cigarette smoke.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cigarette smoke (a known risk factor for cystic fibrosis) causes an increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+, which induces dynamin and calcineurine dependent internalisation of cystic fibrosis tranmsmembrane regulator (CFTR), which is a chloride channel.
cigarette smoke causes a reduction in airway surface liquid (ASL) hydration by inducing dynamin- and Ca2+-dependent internalisation of CF.
the present work provides evidence for an unrecognised role of cytosolic calcium in regulating CFTR plasma membrane expression and function through a mechanism that involves dynamin and calcineurine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CS exposure induces a rise in intracellular calcium which activates calcineurin and causes a reduction in CFTR surface expression.
cigarette smoke exposure induces an increase in intracellular calcium which leads to a dynamin- dependent internalisation of CFRT.
CS exposure to airway cells causes an increase in cytoplasmic calcium, which in turn activates the calcium dependent protein phosphatase calcineurin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
an increase in Ca2+ can induce the internalisation of CF.
Ca2+ can regulate the surface expression of CFTR through a novel mechanism involving the activation of dynamin and calcineurins.
cytosolic calcium is an important regulator of CFTR trafficking, and that this is mediated, at least in part, by calcineurin.
